article.title: Slow Vendor Setup
article.author: Britta Hedlund
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. When a small business wins a contract with a large organization, it often feels like the hard part is over. The proposal was accepted, the price agreed and the work scheduled. Then comes a stage few owners plan for: getting set up as an approved vendor so they can actually be paid. For many small suppliers, that step brings weeks of forms, emails and follow-ups before a first invoice can be processed. For a company with a big cash cushion, the delay is a nuisance. For a small business with payroll due every two weeks, it can be a real strain. How large organizations handle supplier setup has a quiet but direct effect on the smaller firms, and the workers, that depend on them. What Supplier Setup Involves Before a large buyer can pay a new supplier, it needs to collect and confirm several pieces of information. These usually include: Contact details for the business and its billing team. Banking information for receiving payments. Legal identity checks to confirm the company is genuine. Compliance screening, such as checks against sanctions lists. Tax forms and certifications, plus insurance documents where required. Agreed payment terms, so both sides know when invoices are due. Once everything is approved, the supplier's record is created in the buyer's finance system. Only then can invoices move through and payments go out. Where The Process Breaks Down In many organizations, this work still runs through email chains and spreadsheets. A supplier sends documents in whatever format it has. Someone on the buyer's side copies the details into the finance system by hand. Questions go back and forth between procurement, accounts payable and the supplier, often with long gaps between replies. Each handoff creates room for error. A single wrong digit in a bank account number can send a payment to the wrong place. Duplicate supplier records can cause confusion over which details are current. When something goes wrong, there's often no clear record showing where the mistake happened, so fixing it takes even longer. Large organizations feel these problems as extra workload. Accounts payable teams spend a meaningful share of their time answering supplier questions, and many of those questions trace back to setup errors. Small suppliers feel the same problems as missing money. Why Delays Matter More For Small Firms A large corporation can absorb a late payment without much disruption. A small contractor, caterer, cleaning company or local manufacturer often can't. Many small businesses operate on thin margins and pay their staff before their own customers pay them. When a first payment slips by several weeks, owners may dip into savings, delay their own pay, lean on credit or hold off on hiring. A misdirected payment makes things worse. Recovering money sent to the wrong account can take days or weeks, depending on the banks involved. During that time, the supplier has done the work, the buyer believes it has paid, and the people who did the work are still waiting. The Fraud Risk For Everyone Supplier setup is also one of the most common entry points for payment fraud. Criminals often impersonate real vendors and send convincing emails asking a buyer to update bank details. If those changes aren't verified, the next legitimate payment lands in the fraudster's account. Both sides lose. The buyer may have to pay twice or absorb the loss. The real supplier waits even longer for money it has already earned, sometimes while the two companies sort out who's responsible. Unverified banking information is one of the clearest weak points in the entire process of buying and paying for goods and services. How Digital Tools Change The Picture Supplier onboarding software replaces much of the manual back-and-forth with a structured, self-service process. Instead of emailing documents, a new vendor registers through a secure portal, enters its own contact and banking details and uploads the required paperwork. The system checks the data as it's entered, runs compliance screening automatically and routes the registration to the right people for approval. Once approved, verified details flow into the buyer's finance system without being retyped. The same approach applies when details change. Suppliers can update their own banking or address information, but those updates go through the same verification and approval steps as the original registration. That makes it much harder for a fraudulent request to slip through. For suppliers, the practical benefits are fewer emailed requests, faster setup and quicker access to first payment. Many portals also let vendors submit invoices and check payment status themselves, rather than calling or emailing to ask where their money is. Setup that once took weeks can often be finished within hours to a few business days. What Buyers Can Do Organizations that work with many small suppliers can take several steps to make the process fairer and faster: Give new vendors one clear channel for registration. Ask only for the information each type of supplier actually needs. Verify every bank detail change through a trusted contact. Track how long setup takes from contract to first payment. Let suppliers check invoice and payment status on their own. Measuring the time from contract signature to first payment is especially revealing. Many organizations have never looked at that number, and it often shows where delays build up. What Small Suppliers Can Do Small businesses can protect themselves too. Keeping tax forms, insurance certificates and banking letters ready in digital form speeds up registration with any new customer. Asking early about payment terms and setup requirements avoids surprises. Owners should also treat any request to change bank details with caution, whether it comes to them or is made in their name, and confirm such requests by phone with a known contact. A Shared Interest In Getting It Right Supplier setup can seem like routine administrative work, but it shapes how quickly small businesses get paid and how safely money moves between organizations. When the process is slow and error-prone, smaller firms and their employees often bear the cost. When it's clear, verified and largely self-service, buyers reduce their own workload and risk, and suppliers get paid for their work on time. That outcome serves both sides of every contract.
